title: More, Fewer or the Same
short: Match or count to compare two groups.
trouble: Children say the group that is more spread out has more, even when it has fewer objects.

blocks.html: You know how to count how many. Now let’s compare two groups. Which one has more?

blocks.name: counters
blocks.cap: Which row has more? Press “Match them up” to pair each top star with a bottom star.

blocks.html: Match one from each group. The group with extras has more. The other has fewer. If nothing is left over, they are the same.
Matching pairs things up like partners. A thing with no partner is extra, so its group has more.

blocks.title: Apples and pears
blocks.q: There are 6 apples and 4 pears. Which has more?
steps: Match each pear with an apple.
There are more apples and fewer pears.

blocks.name: k-pic
blocks.cap: The stars are spread out, but there are still fewer stars. Count both rows to check.

blocks.html: Saying the longer, more spread-out row has more. Spreading things out does not add any! Match them up, or count both groups.
For grown-ups: Set out two rows of coins, one row spread out. Ask which has more, then match them up together to check.

sources.name: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, Kindergarten, K.CC.C.6: tell whether one group has more than, fewer than or the same as another, by matching or counting
Institute of Education Sciences practice guide: Teaching Math to Young Children (NCEE 2014-4005)
